newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Voters focus on economic woes in Romania poll.
newsitem.headline: Voters focus on economic woes in Romania poll.

text.p: Romanians voted on Sunday in a tight contest between the cautious policies of ex-communist President Ion Iliescu and opposition pledges to tackle poverty with swift economic reform.

Iliescu has ruled Romania since Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was deposed and shot in 1989. Despite opposition criticism that he has done little to end communist-era decay he holds a slight lead in opinion polls.
But his Party of Social Democracy (PSDR), reviled by many for recurrent corruption scandals, trails in the parliamentary race. Iliescu could face a hostile assembly if he wins.
"I regard these elections as a normalisation of the general climate and the general political development of our country," Iliescu told Reuters after after he and his wife Nina voted.
His comments were directed at Western suspicions of the democratic credentials of his administration and opposition allegations of mass attempts to rig the outcome.
Romania's campaign to join NATO and the European Union depends on a free and fair election. It is the only east European state where anti-communists have not been in power.
Iliescu made no prediction on the outcome but said, like most analysts, that a run-off would be needed later this month.
Winner of 1990 and 1992 elections, the president portrays himself as a bulwark of stability against economic decline and conflicts afflicting neighbouring Bulgaria and Yugoslavia.

Many of the 17 million voters appear disgusted at soaring prices, charges of ruling party incompetence and an economic slump that has pushed living standards well below those of near neighbours Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic.
At least one top official seemed ready to abandon Iliescu.
The head of the SRI Intelligence service, successor to Ceausescu's dreaded Securitate police, told state news agency Rompres he wanted to quit his job after the election.
"I will be voting for change," said Virgil Magureanu. Opposition leaders hope voters will do the same.
"I haven't eaten in three days and I'm here to make sure things change," an unemployed man told local television as he waited for polling stations to open.
Iliescu's rivals, CDR leader Emil Constantinescu and ex-prime minister Petre Roman of the Social Democratic Union (USD), have gained ground.
Both push tax cuts, honest government and faster market reforms, but have shied from an election alliance.
Constantinescu predicted victory after voting with his wife and two children in a district of drab apartment blocks.
"Power today is in the hands of Romania's citizens," he said. "I am sure we all know how to use this power for the country's good."
Roman and his family found their names were not on the voters list -- a sign of the chaotic organisation bound to lead to allegations of vote fixing. He voted on a "special list".
Election officials said turnout six hours after polls opened, stood at 20.86 percent on a day of brilliant sunshine. They forecast a high final figure of 75-80 percent.
Although voting ends officially at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT), stations could be kept open until midnight. Exit polls will quickly follow and official results are due late on Monday.
Among early voters were many of Romania's 104,000 army conscripts, who endure tough 12-month stints in uniform.
"I voted for a change that's for sure," Corporal Danut Raducanu said at his base on the outskirts of Bucharest. "I want a job when I come out of here next February."
